text: Walter Brennan had rehearsed the sentence in the shower, then again while shaving, and still his mouth went dry when he saw Mrs. Okafor kneeling in her tulip bed. He crossed the lawn slowly, rolling the survey map into a tighter and tighter tube until the paper creased. "Morning, Adaeze. I was wondering, um, if you had a minute." She sat back on her heels and smiled, which somehow made it worse. He cleared his throat twice. The fence, he explained, would run right along the line, the contractor said, though of course he'd want her opinion, and if she hated the idea he could think again, maybe. He heard himself talking too fast and couldn't slow down. His thumb kept worrying the rubber band on the map. When she asked how tall, he said six feet and immediately added that five would be fine too, or four, whatever looked friendliest. Sweat gathered under his collar even though the morning was cool. He kept glancing at her face for the tiniest tightening of her jaw, bracing for it, already composing an apology for something she hadn't yet said.

I knew Priya had seen the stakes. They went in Saturday, little orange flags snapping along the edge of her driveway, and every time I passed the kitchen window I checked whether she was standing out there looking at them. On Monday I baked banana bread, which I never do, and stood on her porch holding it like a shield. My knuckle hovered at the door for a long moment before I knocked, too softly, then louder, then worried the second knock sounded aggressive. While I waited I counted the bricks in her step. Seven. When she opened the door I blurted, "It's about the fence," before hello, and felt my face go hot. I'd printed the plans. I'd also printed the county regulations, a letter from the surveyor, and a photo of the wood stain, because I'd lain awake at two in the morning imagining every objection she could raise. My voice wobbled on the word "property." I kept shifting my weight from one foot to the other, the bread growing warm and damp against my chest, waiting for her expression to decide what kind of week I was going to have.

The surveyor's van pulled up at nine, and Hiroshi Tanaka watched it from behind the living room curtain, a cold mug of tea forgotten in his hand. Next door, the Delgado family's shutters were still closed. He'd left a note in their mailbox on Thursday and heard nothing back, and that silence had stretched across the whole weekend like a held breath. Was it rude, the note? Too formal? He'd signed it with his full name, which now seemed cold. He stepped onto the porch, retreated, stepped out again. The surveyor waved. Hiroshi waved back and then looked at the Delgados' door as if it might fly open with shouting. His stomach had been tight since breakfast; he hadn't managed more than half a slice of toast. When the surveyor hammered the first pin into the ground, the sound rang out across both yards, and Hiroshi flinched, half expecting a window to slide up. He found himself straightening a flowerpot that didn't need straightening, then another, keeping his hands busy, keeping his eyes on that door.

Grandma Lucille had lived beside the Fenwicks for thirty-one years, and in all that time there'd never been anything between their yards but a row of lilacs. So when Greg Fenwick came over with a clipboard, she felt her heartbeat climb into her throat before he'd even reached the porch. She fussed with the screen door latch, which stuck as it always did, and laughed a little too high when it finally gave. "Come in, come in, mind the cat." She offered coffee, then lemonade, then cookies, getting up twice to fetch things neither of them needed. Greg talked about his new puppy and the gaps under the lilacs, and Lucille nodded and nodded, her fingers pleating and unpleating the hem of her cardigan. Would they take out the lilacs? Her late husband had planted those. She wanted to ask and couldn't quite make her mouth form the question. Instead she asked whether the puppy had a name. Twice. She knew she'd asked twice. Her cheeks burned, and under the table her foot tapped against the chair leg, steady and quick.

I'm the one who wants the fence, which somehow makes it harder. Dmitri next door is a big quiet man who fixes motorcycles in his garage, and I've never once seen him smile. For two weeks I put off talking to him. I'd see his garage door rise and I'd suddenly need to be inside, doing laundry, checking email, anything. Finally my wife said, "Just go," and I went, wiping my palms on my jeans the entire length of the driveway. The radio in his garage was playing something loud and Russian. I stood at the edge of the concrete, not wanting to step in uninvited, and called his name. He didn't hear. I called louder and my voice cracked like I was fourteen. He turned off the radio, wiped his hands on a rag, and waited. I started explaining and lost my place halfway, backtracked, started over. My heart was thudding so hard I could feel it in my ears. I kept saying "if that's okay" at the end of every sentence, like a hiccup I couldn't switch off.

Carmen Ruiz paced the kitchen with her phone in hand, rereading the text she'd drafted to the couple next door. Hi! Hope you're well. We were thinking about putting up a fence along the side yard and wanted to check with you first. She deleted the exclamation point. Added it back. Deleted "we were thinking" because it sounded like a done deal, then worried "we're considering" sounded like she was hiding something. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago. Outside, the neighbors' kids were tossing a frisbee exactly where the posts would go, and every shriek of laughter made her chest tighten a notch. What if they thought she didn't want their children near her yard? What if this was the thing that turned friendly waves into stiff nods for the next twenty years? She pressed send, then flipped the phone face down on the counter and walked away from it. Thirty seconds later she was back, turning it over, staring at the screen, chewing the inside of her cheek until it stung.

The envelope had the property management logo in the corner, and Marcus Bell held it at arm's length as if it might bite. He'd been late on rent once, in March, by three days. They'd said it was fine. Had it been fine? He set the letter on the counter and walked to the window and came back. His heart was going fast and light, the way it did before a job interview. He picked it up again, turned it over, and studied the flap as if the glue could tell him something. Rent increase, probably. Or they were selling the building. Or someone had complained about the bike in the hallway. He ran through every possibility while his thumb traced the edge of the paper. His apartment suddenly felt borrowed, every scuff on the wall a piece of evidence. Finally he slid a butter knife under the flap, his hand not entirely steady, and unfolded the page with a breath held so long it made him lightheaded.

I found it taped to my door, not mailed, which felt worse. Taped, like a notice. Like an eviction in a movie. My key missed the lock twice because I was staring at it. Inside, I put down my groceries without unpacking them and sat on the arm of the couch, the letter in my lap. The ice cream was going to melt. I didn't care. My name was typed across the front, Ms. Ananya Rao, Unit 4C, and the formality of it made my stomach turn over. I'd been running a space heater in January even though the lease technically said not to. Did they know? Could they know? I imagined the super walking past, smelling hot dust under the door. I peeled the tape off carefully, as if being gentle with it would help my case. My mouth tasted like metal. I read the first line three times before the words made sense, my eyes jumping ahead and back, searching for words like terminate or violation before I let myself read anything else.

Old Mr. Kowalski had rented the same two rooms above the bakery for nineteen years, and the new landlord had never once introduced himself. So when the letter came, crisp and white with a law firm's name stamped in blue, he set it beside the kettle and didn't touch it. He made tea instead. He drank the tea standing up, glancing sideways at the envelope every few seconds. His hand trembled slightly when he lifted the cup, and he told himself it was the cold. Downstairs, the bakery's ovens clanged, and for once the smell of bread didn't comfort him. Where would he go? Everything in the neighborhood cost twice what he paid. He rinsed the cup, dried it, put it away, then took it out again for no reason. He sat, stood, adjusted the calendar on the wall. At last he fetched his reading glasses from the bedroom, polished them on his shirt far longer than necessary, and settled into his chair with the letter, his breath shallow and quick.

Jess texted her roommate a photo of the envelope: "did u get one of these??" Then she stared at the three dots that didn't appear. Leah was at work. Of course she was. Jess paced the narrow hallway of their apartment, past the hole in the drywall from the party in September, which they had absolutely not reported. The letter sat on the radiator. Every lap she glanced at it. She picked at her cuticles until one started to bleed and she had to run it under the tap. What if it was about the party? About the noise complaint? About the dog Leah had been fostering that was technically not allowed? The list kept growing. Her chest felt like someone had tightened a strap around it. She opened the fridge, closed it without taking anything, checked her phone again. Still nothing. Finally she grabbed the letter, ripped it open in one jagged motion before she could talk herself out of it, and squeezed her eyes shut for a second before forcing them to read.

I'm forty-six years old and a letter from my landlord still makes my knees go weak. This one arrived certified, which meant I had to sign for it, which meant standing at the post office counter while the clerk slid it across with a bored expression and I scribbled a signature that looked nothing like my own. On the bus home I kept it inside my coat, pressed flat against my ribs, like I was smuggling it. I could feel my pulse against the paper. A teenager across the aisle was laughing at something on her phone, and I envied her completely. I tried to remember the exact date my lease renewed. October? November? My mind went blank. I got off a stop early just to walk, because sitting still had become unbearable. My name is Femi Adeyemi, I've paid on time for six years, I repeated to myself, like a defense attorney rehearsing. At the corner I finally tore it open, my fingers clumsy, the wind trying to snatch the page right out of my grip.

Sophie read the letter once, folded it, and then couldn't remember a single word of it. She unfolded it and read it again. Lease renewal. New terms attached. Please respond by Friday. That was all it said, really, but the attached terms ran four pages, and she sat at the kitchen table with a highlighter, marking every line she didn't understand, which was most of them. Was a 'modified maintenance clause' bad? It sounded bad. Her leg bounced under the table, rattling the salt shaker. She looked up three different legal terms online and each search opened a new set of horror stories. Her cat jumped up onto the table and she pushed it down too sharply, then felt awful and picked it up and held it, its warm weight not quite steadying her. Friday was in three days. She opened her banking app, checked her savings, closed it, checked again as though the number might change. Her throat was tight. She started composing an email to the landlord and deleted the greeting four times.

The departure board flipped from ON TIME to DELAYED, and Elena Vasquez felt her stomach drop as if the plane had already hit turbulence. Her connection in Frankfurt was only seventy minutes. She pulled her boarding pass out of her jacket pocket, studied it, put it back, pulled it out again. Around her, other passengers groaned and shrugged and settled in with their phones, but Elena couldn't sit. She walked to the gate desk, saw the line, walked away, came back and joined it. While she waited she did math in her head, over and over, subtracting the delay from the layover and arriving at numbers that made her palms damp. Her sister's wedding rehearsal was tomorrow evening. She'd promised. She chewed on the zipper pull of her backpack, a habit she thought she'd broken in college. When she reached the counter, her question came out in a rush, too loud, and the agent's calm, practiced voice only made her heart beat faster, because calm was what people used right before bad news.

I've watched the same gate agent pick up her phone four times now. Each time, I sit forward a little, hoping for an announcement, and each time she just nods into the receiver and sets it down. Forty-five minutes delayed has become ninety. My coffee is empty but I keep lifting the cup to my mouth anyway. I'm supposed to present to the board at nine tomorrow morning, in a city I haven't landed in yet, and my slides are on this laptop balanced on my knees, which keep jiggling so much the screen wobbles. The man next to me is asleep with his mouth open. How? I refresh the airline app. I refresh it again. I open my email, compose an apology to my boss, delete it because it feels premature, then write it again. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears and I have to consciously drop them. When the speaker crackles, I nearly knock the cup off the armrest, and my whole body tilts toward the sound, straining to catch every word.

Kwame had never flown alone before. He was nineteen, heading to university abroad, and his mother had cried at security and made him promise to text from every gate. Now the screen said DELAYED and gave no new time, and he didn't know what you were supposed to do. Should he ask someone? Was there a form? Everyone else seemed to know the rules. He stood near the window watching the rain sheet across the tarmac, his passport clutched so tightly the cover was bending. Every few minutes he checked that it was still there, along with his visa letter, flipping the pages to make sure nothing had fallen out. His stomach growled but the thought of food made him queasy. A family nearby argued in a language he didn't recognize, and their raised voices made him flinch. He texted his mother, "delayed, all fine," then stared at the words, unconvinced by them. His thumb hovered over the call button. He didn't press it. He didn't want her to hear his voice.

The pilot had come out of the cockpit to speak to the gate crew, and Ruth Abernathy didn't like that at all. Pilots didn't come out for good news. She was seventy-two and had flown plenty, but lately every mechanical delay sent her mind somewhere dark. She fumbled in her handbag for the peppermints her granddaughter had packed, unwrapped one, and then didn't put it in her mouth. The wrapper crinkled in her fingers until it was a tiny wad. "Maintenance issue," someone near the window said, and the words lodged in her chest. Maintenance on what? She looked at the plane through the glass, its nose pointed patiently at the terminal, and tried to see what might be wrong with it. Her breathing had gone shallow. She made herself count to four on the inhale the way the doctor had shown her, but kept losing track around three. When the boarding announcement finally came, she stayed seated an extra minute, gripping the armrests, watching other people walk calmly down the jet bridge ahead of her.

My daughter's surgery is at seven tomorrow morning, and my flight was supposed to land at eleven tonight. Now it's not boarding until midnight, maybe. Maybe. That's the word the agent used, and I can't stop hearing it. I've called my ex-husband twice to tell him I'm stuck. The second time he said, "You told me already, Jun," not unkindly, and I apologized and hung up and felt my face burn. I keep standing up. I walk to the window, the restroom, the newsstand, where I pick up a magazine and stare at the cover without seeing it. My jaw aches from clenching. I've started compulsively checking other airlines, other routes, other airports two hours from the hospital that I could drive from. None of them work, but I check them again anyway, hoping the numbers will have shifted. A toddler is shrieking two rows over and every shriek scrapes along my spine. I rehearse what I'll say to Mei if I'm not there when she wakes up, and my throat closes around the words.

Theo was flying to meet his girlfriend's parents for the very first time, and the delay gave him three extra hours to think about it. That was the problem. Without the rush of travel to distract him, his mind wandered straight to the dinner table he'd be sitting at tomorrow, the questions about his job, his prospects, the fact that he'd dropped out of law school. He bought a pretzel and ate two bites. He went to the restroom and checked his reflection, smoothed his hair, decided his shirt looked wrinkled, and stood there tugging at the hem as if that would fix it. Back at the gate he practiced introductions under his breath. Mr. Laurent, nice to meet you. Mrs. Laurent, thank you for having me. His voice sounded stiff and fake even to himself. He texted Camille a joke about the delay, then reread it and worried it sounded flippant. When she replied with a heart, he felt a tiny loosening in his chest that lasted maybe four seconds before his knee started bouncing again.

The nurse said the doctor would call by noon. At 11:40, Grace Mbeki was sitting on the edge of her bed with the phone face-up beside her, volume turned all the way up, and she hadn't moved in twenty minutes. Her tea had gone cold on the nightstand. She'd tried to read, gotten through one paragraph four times, and given up. Every car that passed outside made her glance at the phone as if the sound had come from it. Her mind kept circling the word the doctor had used last week, irregular, turning it over the way you'd turn a stone looking for what's underneath. At 11:52 she got up to use the bathroom, then rushed back halfway through washing her hands, convinced she'd missed it. She hadn't. She sat down again, hands wet, and wiped them on her pajama pants. Her heartbeat was loud enough that she could feel it in her fingertips. When the phone finally buzzed, she jumped so hard she knocked it onto the carpet and had to scramble for it.

I logged into the patient portal at 6 a.m. because I couldn't sleep, and there it was: a new result, posted overnight, with a little red flag next to one of the numbers. Red. I stared at that flag for a long time. I didn't know what the number meant. I didn't know what the normal range meant. My finger hovered over the search bar and I knew, I absolutely knew, that searching was a terrible idea. I searched anyway. My breathing got quicker with every link I clicked. One site said it was nothing. Another said it was something. A forum post from 2011 made my chest go tight and cold. My husband was still asleep beside me, and I lay rigid so I wouldn't wake him, holding the phone close to my face under the blanket. My appointment wasn't until Thursday. Three days. I started counting the hours and then made myself stop counting. I kept zooming in on the red flag as if a closer look would change its color.

Arjun Mehta sat across from the oncologist and watched her open the folder. She was taking her time. Why was she taking her time? He was aware of everything at once: the hum of the fluorescent light, the paper crinkling under him on the exam table, the faint antiseptic smell, his own pulse ticking in his neck. His wife held his hand and he could feel that her palm was as damp as his. The doctor put on her glasses. Took them off. Smiled, but it was a careful kind of smile, and Arjun couldn't read it. He found himself studying a poster on the wall about hand-washing, memorizing it, because looking at the doctor's face was too much. His leg was jiggling and he couldn't stop it. When she finally said, "So," and set the folder down, he heard himself let out a short, embarrassing laugh that had nothing to do with anything funny, and his wife squeezed his fingers hard enough to hurt.

Bettina had decided she wouldn't open the envelope until her sister arrived, so it sat on the hall table propped against a vase, the clinic's name printed neatly in the corner. That was an hour ago. Her sister was stuck in traffic. Bettina tidied the living room, which was already tidy. She wiped down the kitchen counter, folded the dish towel into thirds, unfolded it, refolded it into quarters. Every few minutes she drifted back into the hallway and stood over the envelope, not touching it. It was thin. Was thin good? Thin seemed good. Unless thin meant they wanted to tell her in person. She bit her thumbnail down to the quick and then, disgusted with herself, went to find a nail file, and then forgot what she was looking for in the bathroom cabinet. Her mouth was dry no matter how much water she drank. When the doorbell finally rang, her whole body jolted, and she pressed a hand flat against her sternum before she could make herself walk to the door.

The text said: "Your results are ready. Please call the office to schedule a follow-up." I read it at a red light and nearly missed the green. Schedule a follow-up. Not "your results are normal." Not "no further action needed." A follow-up. The car behind me honked and I lurched forward too fast. For the rest of the drive I couldn't hear the radio. I kept running my tongue over my teeth, a habit I get when my mind won't settle. At the office I sat in the parking lot with the engine off and the phone in my lap. My name is Luis Romero, I'm thirty-four, I run every morning. I kept reminding myself of those things as if they were proof of something. I dialed the clinic and hung up before it rang. Dialed again. Got the hold music, a tinny piano version of some pop song, and pressed the phone so hard against my ear that the edge of it left a dent, my other hand gripping the steering wheel.

Mrs. Haddad had not been told what the biopsy might find, only that they were checking, and somehow not knowing what to dread made it worse. In the waiting area she sat very straight with her purse on her knees, both hands on the clasp. Her son had offered to come and she had told him not to be silly, and now she wished she'd said yes. A television in the corner showed a cooking program with the sound off. She watched a chef dice an onion and couldn't have said a moment later what she'd seen. Each time the door to the consultation rooms opened, her head snapped up. Each time it wasn't her name, she let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding. She took out her prayer beads and passed them through her fingers, faster than she meant to, the clicking soft and quick. When the nurse finally called, "Nadia Haddad?" she stood too quickly, her purse sliding off her knees, the contents spilling across the linoleum.

Mr. Delacroix was handing back the tests in alphabetical order, and Zoe Whitfield had never resented her last name more. She watched him move down the rows, papers face down, his expression giving away nothing. Adams. Barker. Chen. Her pencil was wedged between her teeth and she didn't remember putting it there. She'd studied. Hadn't she studied? She'd also skipped the last chapter review because of the swim meet, and question seven had been from that chapter, and she'd guessed. Maybe question nine too. Her stomach felt hollow and fizzy at the same time. Molina. Patel. Each paper landed with a soft slap that she felt in her chest. When he got to the row in front of her, she wiped her palms on her jeans and sat on her hands. Then she pulled them out, because that looked weird. He reached her desk and set the paper down without a word, and for a full ten seconds she couldn't bring herself to flip it over, staring at the blank back as if she could see through it.

I knew it was bad the moment Professor Ingram asked me to stay after class. Everyone else filed out with their exams, and I stood by the whiteboard with my backpack on one shoulder, shifting my weight, trying to look casual and failing. She was sorting papers. Taking forever. My mouth was so dry I kept swallowing nothing. I'm on scholarship. I can't drop below a B average. That fact sat in my throat like a stone. She finally pulled out a single exam, mine, and I saw red ink covering the first page before she even handed it to me. My hand shook when I took it. I hated that she could see it shaking. "Sit down, Malik," she said, gently, and the gentleness frightened me more than anything. I sat. The chair scraped loudly and I winced. I kept my eyes on the paper but couldn't focus on any of the comments, the red lines swimming together, my heart going so fast I thought I might actually be sick right there on her floor.

The exams were in a stack on the corner of Ms. Fujimoto's desk, and Ben spent the entire first half of class staring at that stack instead of the board. Somewhere in there was his midterm, the one he'd finished with eight minutes left and then spent those eight minutes erasing and rewriting the same answer until the paper went thin and gray. His leg was bouncing under the desk so hard that the girl beside him shot him a look. He pressed his heel to the floor. It started again a moment later. When the bell for the second half rang, Ms. Fujimoto picked up the stack and began walking the aisles, and Ben's chest tightened so suddenly he had to take a long breath through his nose. He picked at a loose thread on his hoodie sleeve until it came free and he had a long blue string wrapped around his finger, cutting off the circulation. He didn't notice until the tip went white. Then the paper landed on his desk, and he couldn't breathe properly at all.

Rosalind had graded thousands of papers in her years as a teacher, but this time she was the one waiting for one. At fifty-three, she'd gone back for her nursing certificate, and her pharmacology final was being returned today. She sat in the back row of the lecture hall surrounded by twenty-year-olds who seemed entirely unbothered, laughing and scrolling. She had brought a thermos of tea she was too wound up to drink. She kept smoothing her skirt over her knees, a gesture her mother used to make, she realized, before church. What if she'd made a fool of herself? What if everyone had been right, her brother, her old colleagues, that it was too late for this? The instructor called names. Rosalind's fingers tightened around the thermos until the metal felt warm. When her name came, she stood a little too quickly, bumped her knee on the desk, and walked to the front feeling everyone's eyes on her back, even though, when she glanced around, no one was looking.

Our teacher has a rule: she writes your grade on the last page, so you have to flip through all your mistakes before you find out. I used to think it was funny. Today, holding my chemistry test, I wanted to scream. I'm Lucía, I sit by the window, and the sun was hitting the paper so brightly I could see the ghosts of red marks through the back of every page. So many marks. I turned the first page slowly. Two checks, one X. Second page, an X so big it went off the margin. My face got hot. My heart was hammering and I could hear it, like it was in my ears instead of my chest. My best friend Paula leaned over and whispered, "What'd you get?" and I shook my head without looking at her. I didn't know yet. I didn't want to know yet. I pinched the corner of the last page between two fingers and held it there, not turning it, just feeling the paper go damp under my fingertips.

The tutor had promised to bring Owen's graded essay to their Tuesday session, and Owen had arrived at the library twenty minutes early. He'd chosen a table near the door so he could see her come in. Then he'd moved to a table by the window, where she wouldn't see him first. Then back. He arranged his pens in a straight line, then into a fan, then back into his bag. The essay was the one his whole application depended on, the writing sample he'd been told could make or break his transfer. Every time the door swung open his shoulders jumped. A man with a stroller. A girl with headphones. Not her. He drank half his water bottle and then needed the bathroom and didn't dare go. His jaw was clenched so tightly it ached behind his ears. When he finally spotted her coming through the turnstile with a folder under her arm, he stood up out of reflex, sat back down, and found his hands had gone cold despite the heat of the radiator beside him.

Naomi spotted him by the avocados and immediately turned her cart around, then stopped in the middle of the aisle, blocking an elderly man with a basket. It was definitely Caleb. Same slouch, same way of squinting at labels. They hadn't spoken in eleven years, not since the falling-out over the apartment and the security deposit and all the things they'd both said. She muttered an apology to the man with the basket and pretended to study a display of canned tomatoes, her heart going hard and fast. Should she leave? Her ice cream was already in the cart. She could abandon the cart. People did that. Her cheeks were burning. She picked up a can, read the ingredients without absorbing a single word, put it down. Out of the corner of her eye she saw him turning toward her aisle, and every muscle in her back went tight. She smoothed her hair, realized she was wearing her oldest sweatpants, and felt her stomach clench into a small, hard knot just as he looked up.

"Rahul? Rahul Kapoor?" I heard my own name from somewhere behind the deli counter and my whole body went stiff. I turned around holding a pound of sliced turkey and there was Deepa, my best friend from engineering college, who I'd stopped answering texts from about four years ago for reasons I still couldn't explain, even to myself. She was smiling. She looked genuinely pleased. That made it worse. I smiled back and felt it come out crooked. "Wow, hey, wow," I said, three times, like an idiot. My free hand went to the back of my neck and stayed there. She asked what I was doing these days and I gave a long, rambling answer, too many details, too fast, because if I kept talking she couldn't ask why I'd disappeared. The deli guy called the next number. I kept squeezing the turkey package until the plastic crinkled loudly. I could feel sweat starting under my arms, and I kept glancing toward the checkout lanes as though measuring how far away the exit was.

Marguerite almost didn't recognize Joan at first. The hair had gone white, and she leaned on the cart like a walker now. But the laugh, when Joan laughed at something the cashier said, was exactly the same, and it went through Marguerite like a bell. They had been inseparable at seventeen. Then Joan had married Marguerite's brother, and the divorce had been ugly, and the family had picked sides. Marguerite had picked her brother's. She stood frozen by the bread shelf, a loaf of rye clutched against her coat. Her fingers were pressing dents into the bag. Should she go over? What would she even say? Sorry I sided with Frank for thirty years? She swallowed and felt her throat click. Her heart was doing a strange, skippy rhythm that she'd have to mention to her doctor. She took one step toward the registers and stopped, took another, and felt her knees go loose and unreliable beneath her, as if they too were unsure whether they wanted to carry her any closer.

It's strange how the body knows before the mind does. I was reaching for a carton of eggs when my hand just stopped, midair, because across the aisle was Tomás, and my pulse leapt before I'd even fully registered his face. We'd shared a dorm room for three years. He'd been at my wedding. I hadn't been at his, because I'd been too busy, which was a lie, and he knew it was a lie. He hadn't seen me yet. I could still slip away. Instead I stood there with the fridge door open and cold air rolling over my arms, raising goosebumps, and I couldn't decide anything at all. My mouth was suddenly dry. When he turned and our eyes met, his face did something complicated, and I said, "Hey, man," in a voice that came out about an octave higher than my real one. I let the fridge door swing shut too hard. The eggs rattled in my basket, and I grabbed it tighter to make them stop, my knuckles going pale around the handle.

Yuki had moved back to her hometown after the divorce, and she'd known this would happen eventually, but not on a Saturday morning at the supermarket with no makeup and a cart full of frozen dinners for one. Haruka from high school was standing at the end of the aisle, polished and bright, two kids hanging off her cart. Yuki pivoted toward the cereal and stared at a box of oatmeal as though it held urgent news. Her neck prickled. She was sure Haruka had seen her. The kids were getting louder, closer. Yuki's grip tightened on the cart handle until the plastic creaked. She thought about everything Haruka might ask: what are you doing back here, how's your husband, what happened. Each question landed in her stomach like a dropped stone. She pushed the cart forward without picking anything up, then back again, a pointless little shuffle. When she heard her name called, bright and surprised, she flinched visibly and then turned with a smile so wide it made her cheeks hurt.

Gabriel recognized the tattoo first, a faded swallow on the inside of a wrist reaching for a jar of peanut butter, and then he recognized the arm, and then the face. Lena. His old bandmate. The one he'd left behind when he signed that solo deal and never called again. He ducked behind a pyramid of soda bottles, absurdly, like a cartoon spy, then felt ridiculous and stepped out again. His pulse was ticking fast in his throat. She'd been the better guitarist; everyone said so. He still owed her an apology, maybe money, definitely an explanation. He fumbled with the shopping list on his phone, scrolled up and down without reading it. The fluorescent lights felt suddenly too bright, every hum of the freezers too loud. He rehearsed an opening line: Hey, crazy running into you. No. Lena, I've been meaning to call. Worse. When she rounded the corner straight toward him, his mind went perfectly blank, and all he managed was to lift one hand in a stiff, half-finished wave.

The dashboard lit up like a Christmas tree, and then the engine just quit, right there in the middle lane of the interstate. Felipe wrenched the wheel toward the shoulder, the car coasting, losing speed, horns blaring behind him. He made it onto the gravel and sat gripping the wheel with both hands, breathing hard. It was 8:12. His first day on the new job started at nine. He turned the key. Nothing but a click. He turned it again, harder, as if force would help. Click. Trucks roared past so close the whole car shuddered with each one, and he flinched every time. He grabbed his phone and dropped it into the footwell, and when he fished it out his fingers were trembling too much to unlock it on the first try. Who did you call? His new boss? A tow truck? Both? His shirt was sticking to his back. He kept glancing at the clock on the dash, which kept stubbornly moving forward, and at the side mirror, which kept filling with oncoming headlights.

I heard the noise before anything else, a metallic clatter from under the hood like someone had dropped a wrench in a blender. Then steam, lots of it, pouring up over the windshield. I pulled into a gas station I'd never seen before and coasted to a stop by the air pump. The attendant was watching me through the window. I sat there with my hands frozen on the wheel. My name is Ingrid, I'm a dental hygienist, and I have three patients booked before ten, and I know absolutely nothing about cars. I didn't know if steam meant the car might explode. I unbuckled my seatbelt and got out fast, then stood a few feet away, hugging my elbows. The cold air was biting but my face felt hot. I called my office and got voicemail and left a message that rambled so badly I wanted to delete it. Then I called my dad, who didn't answer either. I paced in a little circle by the pump, glancing at the hood every few seconds, half expecting flames.

Mustafa had been late twice already this month, and his supervisor had made a point of mentioning it in front of the whole crew. So when the old sedan started juddering on the bridge and then died completely, rolling to a stop with the hazards blinking, the first thing he felt wasn't frustration. It was a sharp, hot clench in his gut. He sat in the dead car on the bridge, traffic squeezing around him, and stared at the phone in his hand. He had to call. He couldn't call. He typed a text instead, deleted it, typed another one. Every phrase sounded like an excuse, even though it was true. He pressed the hazard button again even though it was already on, just to do something with his hands. His mouth had gone dry, and he kept licking his lips. A bus went by, and he saw passengers staring down at him through the windows, and he sank lower in the seat, wishing the whole car could just disappear into the river below.

The car made it to the edge of the school parking lot and stopped. Just stopped. Joanne pumped the gas pedal and nothing happened, and in the back seat her six-year-old asked, "Mommy, why aren't we moving?" She said, "It's fine, baby," brightly, too brightly. It wasn't fine. She had to drop him at school and then drive thirty minutes to the hospital where she was supposed to start her shift at eight, and the charge nurse had already warned her about the schedule. She got out, popped the hood, and stared at the engine as if it might explain itself. It didn't. Her hands were cold and she shoved them into her coat pockets, then pulled them out to check her phone, then shoved them back. Other parents were pulling in around her, waving, and she waved back with a tight little smile. She could feel a headache building behind her eyes. She walked her son to the school door, kissed his hair, and as soon as he was inside her chin started trembling.

Nobody tells you how quiet it gets when your engine dies on a country road. I was halfway between my village and the city, fog lying thick in the ditches, and suddenly the only sounds were birds and the tick of cooling metal. My phone showed one bar of signal, flickering. I held it up toward the sky, toward the trees, toward the windshield, chasing that bar like it was oxygen. I'm Ola, I work at the bank, and today was the quarterly audit, the one I'd prepped for all month, the one my manager had said I absolutely could not miss. My stomach turned over every time I looked at the clock. I tried the ignition again and the starter whined and gave up, and I slapped the steering wheel and then immediately felt bad, as if the car could be offended. A tractor appeared far down the road, coming slowly, and I didn't know whether to flag it down or hide. I stood beside the car with one arm half raised, unsure, my heart pounding in the stillness.

Seo-yeon pulled the dead car onto the shoulder of the expressway and sat for a full minute without moving, staring at the glowing orange warning light as if it had personally betrayed her. Today was the client pitch. She'd rehearsed it in the shower, in the mirror, on the drive itself until the engine started coughing. Now her slides were on the laptop beside her, and the client's office was eleven kilometers away, and the car would not start. She called a taxi app and watched the little spinning wheel, which spun and spun. Her foot was tapping the floor mat so fast it made a soft rhythmic thump. She checked her makeup in the visor mirror, though it hadn't changed, and noticed a faint shine of sweat on her upper lip. She dabbed it with a tissue, then dabbed it again. When a driver finally accepted, she grabbed her bag and the laptop and nearly forgot her phone on the seat, and she had to stand outside the car, keys in hand, breathing deep and slow to stop her shoulders from shaking.

Midnight came and went, and Dolores was still sitting in the armchair by the front window with every light in the house on. Curfew had been eleven. She had texted Sofia at 11:15, 11:30, 11:45. The messages sat there, delivered, unread. She told herself that teenagers lost track of time, that phones died, that this happened in every family. She told herself this several times. Her knitting lay in her lap, the needles still, the same row half finished for an hour. Every time headlights swept across the ceiling she leaned forward, her whole body straining toward the glass, and every time the car passed she sank back. Her stomach was a hard, sour ball. She got up and checked the back door, which was locked, and the side door, also locked, and then the back door again. She refilled her tea and didn't drink it. At 12:20 she picked up the phone to call Sofia's friend's mother, then put it down, afraid of seeming overbearing, then picked it up again, her thumb hovering over the name.

I've been listening to the house for an hour. Every creak, every gust against the gutters, I sit up in bed thinking it's the front door. It isn't. My son is sixteen and he has his license now, which seemed like such a happy milestone in June. He was supposed to be home at eleven-thirty. It's quarter to one. My wife fell asleep around twelve, telling me not to worry, but she slept facing the door with her phone on the pillow next to her. I've checked the location app so many times that my battery is at nine percent. It shows Isaiah's phone at a friend's house, the same pin, unmoving for ninety minutes. Why isn't it moving? I keep replaying every news story about teenage drivers. I can't stop. My chest is tight like I've been holding my breath, and I realize I have. I get up, pull on a robe, and stand in the dark hallway looking down the stairs at the front door, listening so hard my ears ring, willing the lock to turn.

Kofi had promised himself he wouldn't be the kind of father who waited up, but here he was at the kitchen table at one in the morning, the overhead light buzzing faintly, a cold cup of coffee in front of him. Ama had gone to a concert in the city with three friends. She'd texted at ten: "So good!!" and nothing since. He kept reading that text, as if two exclamation points could tell him where she was now. He'd washed every dish in the sink. He'd wiped the counters twice. He'd started reorganizing the spice rack, alphabetically, and stopped at cumin because his hands had become too fidgety to manage the small jars. Outside, a siren wailed somewhere distant, and he went completely still, listening as it faded, his pulse loud in his ears. He picked up the phone and called her. It rang and rang and went to voicemail, her cheerful recorded voice saying leave a message. He hung up without leaving one, then immediately called again, gripping the phone hard enough to hurt.

The porch light was on. Brigid had turned it on at nine, and it was the only light now on the whole street, a yellow island swarming with moths. She sat on the bottom stair inside the front hall in her dressing gown, her back against the banister, knees drawn up. Liam was seventeen, and he'd been so quiet lately, so closed, and he'd left tonight without saying where. She'd heard the car door slam. That was all. Now it was two in the morning. She kept thinking of the quarrel they'd had last week, the things she'd shouted, and imagining it was the last thing she'd said to him. Her throat squeezed. She kept turning her wedding ring around and around her finger, though her husband had been gone five years and there was no one else awake to hear her. When a car finally slowed outside, she sprang to her feet so fast she got dizzy, and she had to steady herself on the wall, staring at the frosted glass, holding her breath.

I'm on the couch with the TV muted, a nature documentary playing that I haven't actually watched. Penguins, I think. My daughter Rosa said she'd be back from the party by midnight. It's twelve-forty. I keep telling myself forty minutes is nothing, she's fifteen, she probably didn't check her phone. But my knee won't stop bouncing, and I've chewed the skin around my thumbnail raw. I've looked out the front window so many times that the neighbor's motion-sensor light keeps flicking on when I move the curtain. I texted her mom's friend whose house the party was at, and that felt like such a huge, embarrassing step, and she hasn't answered either. That's worse. Now two people aren't answering. I stand up and sit down. I go to the fridge, open it, stare at the shelves, close it. A car door slams somewhere down the block and I'm at the window instantly, my forehead nearly touching the cold glass, my breath fogging a little circle, peering into the dark for a familiar shape walking up the drive.

Anton had his coat on. He'd put it on at 12:30 and had been standing in the hallway in it ever since, car keys in hand, not quite able to decide whether to go looking or keep waiting. Mischa had gone to a friend's to study, supposedly. The friend's parents weren't answering. Anton jingled the keys, a fast metallic chatter in the silent house, then closed his fist around them to stop the sound. His wife was on a night shift and he didn't want to call her and frighten her over nothing. If it was nothing. He walked to the kitchen and back, his footsteps loud on the old floorboards, and caught sight of himself in the hallway mirror, pale and hollow-eyed under the lamp. He looked older than he felt, or maybe exactly as old as he felt right now. A dog barked down the road and he froze, head cocked, listening. Footsteps? No. The dog stopped. He opened the front door anyway and stood on the cold step, keys biting into his palm, staring at the empty street.

"Can you pop into my office for a second?" Diane said, and walked away before Kevin could answer. Pop in. A second. Casual words, but she hadn't smiled, and she'd closed her laptop before she said it. Kevin sat at his desk and stared at the cursor blinking in his half-finished email. His heart rate had picked up so suddenly it was almost funny. He saved the email. He stood up, sat back down, opened his calendar to see if he'd missed some meeting. Nothing. He thought about the Q3 report, the typo he'd caught too late, the client who'd seemed annoyed on Thursday's call. He thought about the layoffs at the other branch. He grabbed a notepad and a pen, because walking in empty-handed felt unprofessional, then wondered if bringing a notepad would look like he was expecting bad news. The walk to her office was twenty steps and it felt like a mile. He could feel his coworkers glancing up. At her door, he raised his hand to knock and noticed the tremor in his fingers.

The calendar invite just said "Quick chat" and it was set for 4:45 on a Friday. If you've ever worked in an office, you know what that means. I spent the whole afternoon pretending to work. I opened spreadsheets and scrolled them without seeing. I went to the break room three times for water I didn't drink. My stomach was so knotted I skipped lunch. My name is Amara and I've been at this company for six years, and I kept listing my accomplishments to myself like a lawyer preparing closing arguments. I'd trained half the new hires. I'd landed the Henderson account. Did any of that count? At 4:40 I went to the restroom and stared at myself in the mirror. I straightened my blazer, then took it off, then put it back on. My face looked pale and pinched. I practiced a neutral expression. At 4:44 I was standing outside his door, and I could hear him on the phone, laughing, and I didn't know whether that laugh was a good sign or a terrible one.

Pedro was stocking shelves when the floor supervisor came and told him the manager wanted him in the back. Right now. He set down the box of cereal so carefully you'd think it was glass, and walked toward the back of the store with his apron still on, his heart pounding against his ribs. He'd been working here for four months. He needed this job. His mother's rent depended on it. He tried to think what he'd done wrong. The register had been five dollars short last Tuesday; he'd counted twice. Had they found out? Did they think he'd taken it? His face went hot at the thought. He wiped his palms on his apron and found it didn't help; they were damp again immediately. The door to the manager's office was propped open and he could see her at the desk, writing something. He hovered at the threshold, not sure whether to knock on an open door. He knocked on the frame, very lightly, and his knuckles barely made a sound.

Harriet had been managing people for twenty years and she knew the script. You call someone in, you close the door, you say "have a seat." So when her own new director, ten years younger, said "Harriet, have a seat," and closed the door behind her, every alarm bell in her body went off at once. She sat. She crossed her legs, uncrossed them, set her hands primly on her knees. There was a folder on his desk. There was a box of tissues beside it. Was that box always there? Her mouth went dry and she swallowed several times, too loudly, she was sure. He was saying something about restructuring and she nodded along, but she wasn't really hearing the words, just watching his hands, waiting for them to open the folder. Her heart was beating in her temples. She noticed a small chip in the paint on the wall behind him and fixed her eyes on it, the way she'd once fixed her eyes on the ceiling at the dentist, waiting for the drill.

I saw my manager walk past my desk with HR. Then, fifteen minutes later, my phone buzzed with a message: "Got a minute? My office." I'm going to be honest, I seriously considered hiding in the stairwell. I'm Callum, I'm twenty-four, and this is my first real job after university. I'd made a mistake on the payroll file last week, a small one, I'd fixed it, but now I couldn't stop thinking about it. I stood up and my chair rolled backward and hit the filing cabinet with a bang. Everyone turned. My face went scarlet. I walked to the office with my arms stiff at my sides like a toy soldier, then tried to loosen them, then didn't know what to do with my hands at all. I shoved them in my pockets. Took them out. The office door was closed, and I could see two shapes through the frosted glass. My heart was going so fast I felt slightly sick. I knocked, and the door swung open before my knuckles even landed a second time.

Wen Li's manager emailed at 7 a.m.: "Come see me when you're in. No rush." She read it on the train and spent the next forty minutes rereading it. No rush. Why add no rush? People only said no rush when something was serious enough that they needed to soften it. She stared out the window at the gray buildings sliding past without seeing them. Her coffee went cold in her hand. She went through the last month in her head, every meeting, every comment, every deadline. Had she been short with that vendor? Had someone complained? By the time she got off the train her shoulders were up around her ears, and she had to consciously roll them back. In the office elevator she pressed her floor button three times. She went to her desk first, took off her coat, booted up her computer, arranged her pens, putting it off. Then she walked to his door, her steps getting slower as she approached, and stood outside it for a long moment with her hand on the handle.

Simone found the letter wedged in the back of her father's old army footlocker, under a folded wool blanket that smelled of mothballs. The envelope was addressed to her mother, in handwriting Simone didn't recognize, and postmarked 1971, two years before Simone was born. She sat back on her heels in the dusty attic, the single bulb swinging slightly overhead. Her fingertips tingled. Her mother had never mentioned anyone from before her father. Not once. Simone turned the envelope over. The flap had been opened and carefully resealed with tape gone yellow. Someone had read it, then hidden it. She glanced toward the attic stairs, though there was no one in the house to catch her. Her heart was beating hard enough that she could feel it in her throat. She slid one finger under the old tape and then stopped, pulled it back, held the letter in both hands and just looked at it. Did she want to know? Downstairs, the old clock struck, and she flinched at every chime.

I was only supposed to be clearing out boxes for the estate sale. Then I opened a shoebox of my grandfather's and saw my own name on an envelope. Not addressed to me. About me. "Regarding Esteban," written in his careful, slanted hand. I was eight when he died. The attic was stuffy and hot, the air thick with dust motes, and suddenly I couldn't get a full breath. I sat down on a stack of old National Geographics, which slid and nearly toppled me. My hands had gone clammy and I wiped them on my jeans, leaving gray streaks. What could my grandfather have written about me? Something about my father? About the custody fight? I'd always sensed there was a story nobody told me. I held the envelope up to the little attic window and tried to see through it, which was childish, and I knew it was childish, but I couldn't make my fingers open it yet. My heart thudded. Somewhere below, my sister called up, asking if I was okay, and I said "Fine!" much too quickly.

The letter was in an old cigar box with a few photographs and a ribbon, and Hamid knew from the first line that it wasn't meant for him to read. My dearest, it began. It was his father's handwriting. His mother's name was not Leyla. He stopped reading immediately and put it face down on the dusty floorboards, his heart thumping. The attic was quiet except for rain on the roof, a soft insistent drumming that suddenly seemed far too loud. His father had been dead for eight months. His mother was downstairs making lunch. He could hear the clink of plates. He looked at the letter, face down, and then at the hatch to the attic, and back at the letter. His palms were damp. He picked it up again, read one more line, and felt his face grow hot, as if he'd been caught. He folded it in half, then into quarters, and held it pressed between his hands, wondering whether to read it, burn it, or hide it back exactly where it had been.

Claire's flashlight beam caught the corner of a pink envelope sticking out of a hatbox, and she pulled it out without thinking. It was addressed to her, in her own childish handwriting. To Claire, age 30. Open on your birthday. She'd written it at twelve, she now vaguely remembered, a school project. She was thirty-four. She sat down cross-legged on the plywood floor of the attic and held it in her lap. It was ridiculous to feel this way about a letter from herself, but her stomach was fluttering, and her throat had gone tight. What had she hoped for, back then? Who had she thought she'd become? She could guess, and she suspected the gap between that girl's dreams and her life now, divorced and temping and living in her parents' house, would be wide enough to fall into. She turned the envelope over and over. She picked at the stickers on the back, faded unicorns, until one peeled off on her thumb. She took a long breath and still didn't open it.

I knew my mother's handwriting the way you know a voice, and the moment I saw it on the envelope in the bottom of the trunk, I felt my heartbeat change. She'd been gone two years. The letter was addressed to my father, and it was dated the month before he moved out. I'd always been told that was mutual, amicable, just two people growing apart. The attic floor creaked under me as I shifted my weight, and I jumped at the sound. I'm forty-one years old and I jumped. I'm Dev, I'm a pharmacist, I handle things, and here I was unable to handle an envelope. My fingers were cold despite the heat under the roof. I unfolded it halfway and saw the first line, I can't keep pretending, and I folded it back up so fast the paper tore a little at the crease. I stared at that tiny tear and felt sick about it. Dust swirled through the window light and I sat completely still, listening to my own breathing, the letter half open in my lap.

The attic had been sealed for years, and when Ingeborg finally pried the hatch open, the first thing she found was a stack of letters tied with string, all addressed to her great-aunt Hilde, all from a sender named only by initials. The top one had a German stamp and a date in 1944. Ingeborg's chest tightened. Everyone in the family knew there was something about Hilde nobody talked about, a silence that settled over Christmas dinners whenever her name came up. Ingeborg untied the string slowly, as if any sudden movement might bring the past down on her head. The paper was brittle and she was afraid of tearing it, so she held it with just her fingertips, barely breathing. A dog was barking somewhere in the street and each bark made her hands jerk. She read the first word. Then she looked at the attic hatch, open behind her, a square of light, and felt the urge to close it, to make sure no one could come up and see her face while she read.

The doorbell was due to ring in twelve minutes, and the risotto was not behaving. Luca stirred it with one hand and checked the oven with the other, nearly scorching his wrist on the rack. His boyfriend's parents were coming. The parents who had been polite but cool for two years, who had once called his cooking "interesting." He'd chosen risotto because it was his grandmother's recipe and he'd made it a hundred times, but tonight the rice felt grainy and wrong. He tasted it. Tasted it again. Added salt, then panicked that he'd added too much and tasted again, his tongue no longer able to tell anything. Sweat was beading at his hairline from the steam. He wiped it with his sleeve and left a streak of parmesan on his forehead. The roast still needed resting. The salad wasn't dressed. He glanced at the clock on the microwave so often that the numbers seemed to jump ahead every time. When a car door slammed outside, his spoon clattered against the pot.

I've cooked Thanksgiving for my family for fifteen years, but this is the first year my new husband's family is coming, all eleven of them, and the turkey is still pink at the bone. I keep opening the oven door, which I know lets the heat out, which I know makes it worse, and I can't stop. The kitchen is so hot my glasses keep fogging. My name is Bernadette, I teach high school biology, I can explain protein denaturation in my sleep, and right now I could not tell you what temperature poultry is safe at. I've looked it up three times. The gravy has lumps. I'm whisking it so hard my forearm is cramping. My sister-in-law texted twenty minutes ago that they're "just leaving," which means they'll be here any second. I keep catching my reflection in the dark kitchen window, flushed and frazzled, a dish towel slung over my shoulder, and I keep smoothing my hair with fingers that smell of sage and onion. My heart jumps every time a car passes.

Chidi had invited his entire research group for dinner, including his advisor, and he had never cooked for more than two people in his life. The jollof rice was simmering, the chicken was in the oven, and he had seven minutes. He stood in the middle of his tiny kitchen, turning in place, unable to decide what to do first. The plantains. Yes. He sliced them too fast, and the knife skidded and nicked his thumb. He stuck it in his mouth, tasting blood, and with his other hand he flipped through the recipe on his phone, leaving smears of oil across the screen. Was the rice supposed to smell this smoky? His mother's always smelled smoky. Was this the good smoky or the burnt smoky? He lifted the lid, peered in, and couldn't tell. His shirt was sticking to his back. He had the sudden absurd urge to call his mother in Lagos and ask, even though it was the middle of the night there. The buzzer rang downstairs, and his whole body went rigid, a spatula frozen in midair.

Maeve's soufflé had risen beautifully in the oven, and now she was afraid to breathe near it. She crouched in front of the oven door, peering through the smudged glass, while behind her the dining table sat set and gleaming, candles unlit, eight chairs waiting. Her new boss was one of the guests. That was why she'd chosen a soufflé, to impress, and now she understood that was madness. Her knees ached from crouching. She didn't dare stand up in case the movement somehow caused a collapse. The timer said four minutes. She watched the seconds tick down with her teeth sunk into her lower lip. She heard laughter on the street outside, voices getting closer, the click of heels on the pavement, and her stomach gave a hard lurch. Could they be early? Please don't be early. She reached up blindly to the counter for her wine glass and knocked it over, and red wine spread across the white tiles, and she just stared at it, frozen between the spill and the soufflé.

I'd never hosted a dinner party before. I'm twenty-six and I live on cereal and takeout, but my new friends from the climbing gym had somehow ended up invited, and now they were due at seven-thirty and it was seven-twenty and the pasta water still wasn't boiling. I stood over the pot, watching tiny bubbles form on the bottom and refuse to rise. A watched pot, I know. I couldn't look away. I'm Jonah, by the way, and I'd cleaned my apartment for two hours this afternoon, scrubbing grout with a toothbrush, shoving piles of laundry into the closet, and I kept walking out of the kitchen to check that the closet door was still shut. It was. I came back. The sauce was spitting tomato onto the backsplash. I'd bought a fancy bottle of olive oil and couldn't get the cap off. My hands were slippery. I wrenched at it until my palm burned. When my phone buzzed with "on our way up!" I actually said "no, no, no" out loud to an empty kitchen.

Fatima tasted the lamb stew for the sixth time and still couldn't decide if it needed more cumin. Her mother-in-law was coming tonight, for the first time since the wedding, and her mother-in-law was the best cook in three provinces, as everyone in the family reminded her at every opportunity. The kitchen windows had steamed over completely. Fatima's headscarf had slipped back from the heat and she pushed it forward again with the back of her wrist, her fingers sticky with dough from the bread she was shaping. The bread looked lopsided. She reshaped it. It looked worse. Her husband poked his head in to ask if she needed help, and she said "No, everything is perfect," in a voice so high and tight that he raised his eyebrows and slowly backed out. She laid out the serving dishes, rearranged them, swapped the blue bowl for the white one and back again. When she heard a taxi stop outside, she wiped her hands on her apron three times and went to the window, her throat completely dry.

The keys the building manager handed Adebayo were heavier than he'd expected, an old-fashioned iron ring with five keys, and he had no idea which one opened the front door. He stood on the stoop of the brownstone with his two suitcases, trying them one at a time while people streamed past on the sidewalk behind him. The third key stuck. The fourth wouldn't turn. He could feel the back of his neck growing hot. Someone across the street was watching him, or seemed to be. Did he look like he was breaking in? He fumbled the ring, dropped it, and it clanged on the stone step loud as a bell. He'd left his whole life behind in Houston, his job, his friends, his mother's Sunday dinners, for a position he'd accepted over video. What if he'd made a terrible mistake? His pulse was racing. He picked up the keys and tried the fifth, and when it turned, he pushed into the dim hallway and leaned against the door, breathing hard, staring up at the long dark staircase.

The movers left at 6 p.m. and suddenly the apartment was very quiet. I stood in the middle of the living room surrounded by cardboard boxes, and the city noise through the window sounded completely foreign, sirens pitched wrong, a language on the street I could only half understand. I've just moved to Montreal for graduate school, and my French is passable on paper. I'm Hannah. I'm from a small town in Ohio where I knew every single person at the grocery store. Now I didn't even know where the grocery store was. I opened a box, saw it was kitchen stuff, closed it again. I kept going to the window and looking out at the unfamiliar street, then away. My stomach was fluttery and hollow. I hadn't eaten since the airport but the idea of going out, finding somewhere, ordering in a language I'd mostly learned from textbooks, made my chest tighten. I tested the lock on the door. Twice. Then I sat on a box, phone in my lap, and scrolled through my contacts without calling anyone.

Vikram's first night in the new apartment, he couldn't sleep. The building made sounds he didn't recognize: a clank in the radiator, footsteps overhead that stopped and started at odd intervals, the elevator groaning somewhere down the shaft. Each time, his eyes snapped open in the dark. His mattress was on the floor because the bed frame hadn't arrived, and lying so low made him feel exposed, like the room loomed over him. He'd signed a twelve-month lease for this place after seeing it on a video call. The rent was nearly double what he'd paid in Pune. He got up at two and checked that the door was bolted. He drank a glass of water standing at the sink, looking out at an unfamiliar skyline, the lights blinking on a tower he didn't know the name of. He turned over every decision that had brought him here, worrying at each one. His jaw ached; he'd been clenching it. At three he got up again, checked the bolt again, and stood in the dark hallway listening.

The new apartment smelled of fresh paint and somebody else's cooking drifting in from the hallway. Marisol walked through the rooms twice, touching the walls, opening and closing every cupboard door, as if learning them would make the place hers. It didn't. Tomorrow was her first day at the new hospital, in a city of four million where she knew exactly one person, her cousin, who lived an hour away by train. She unpacked her scrubs first and hung them in the closet, then took them down, checked them for wrinkles, hung them back up. She set three alarms on her phone. Then a fourth. Every time she sat down, she found a new thing to do: plug in the lamp, find the light bulbs, look up the bus route again. The bus route. She'd already looked it up five times, but she opened the map anyway and traced the line with her finger, her lips moving silently as she memorized the stops. Her stomach was too knotted to eat the sandwich she'd bought.

On the third day in my new city I still hadn't met any of my neighbors, and I was beginning to dread it. Every time I heard a door in the hallway I froze with my hand on my own doorknob, waiting until the footsteps faded before slipping out. It was absurd. I'm a grown woman, Agnieszka, thirty-eight, a project manager who runs meetings with forty people. But here, in this narrow corridor with its unfamiliar smells and muffled music, I felt about ten years old. This morning I finally ran into the man from next door at the mailboxes. He said good morning. I said good morning back and then, to my horror, kept talking: where I was from, why I'd moved, that I liked his doormat. He nodded politely. My face was burning. I fumbled with the tiny mailbox key and couldn't get it into the lock, and he waited, holding the outer door for me, and I could feel the sweat prickling under my collar as the key scraped and slipped and scraped again.

Tobias carried the last box up the four flights alone, because the friend who had promised to help had cancelled, and he didn't know anyone else in the city. At the top he set it down and stood catching his breath in the doorway of an apartment that didn't feel like his. Through the thin wall he could hear the neighbors arguing in rapid Spanish, then a door slammed. He flinched. His new job started Monday. His savings had gone on the deposit. The checklist on his phone said: set up internet, find a doctor, buy groceries, register address. Each item made his chest feel a little tighter. He opened the fridge to put away the milk he'd bought and found it wasn't cold. Wasn't even humming. He stood there with the door open, staring into the dark interior, and felt the panic climb up his throat. Who did you call about a fridge? Did the landlord fix that? He didn't even have the landlord's number saved. He scrolled through his emails, fingers clumsy, searching.

Mile twenty-five and Ana's left calf had started to twitch in a way she didn't like. Not a cramp yet. A warning. She'd felt that warning in Chicago two years ago, at almost exactly this spot, and twenty minutes later she'd been sitting on the curb with a medic, watching everyone run past. The memory sat on her shoulders like a weight. She shortened her stride. Was that the right call? It slowed her down. Her watch said she was on pace, just barely, for the qualifying time she'd trained eighteen months for. She glanced down at it again, then again, the numbers swimming in her sweat-blurred vision. Every step she waited for the calf to lock. The crowd was screaming, cowbells clanging, someone holding a sign with her name, and she couldn't even look up to see who it was. Her breath was coming in short, ragged pulls that had nothing to do with the running. She tested the leg with each footfall, gingerly, feeling for the seize, her jaw locked tight.

I could see the clock above the finish line from a mile out, and I couldn't stop calculating. Three hours, eleven minutes. If I held this pace, I'd come in just under three-fifteen. If I slowed even a little, I'd miss it. My name is Grant and I'm forty-four and this is my sixth attempt at a Boston qualifier, and I'm not sure my knees have a seventh in them. Every split I watched my watch like it was a bomb timer. My legs felt like they belonged to someone else, heavy and distant, and every time I swung one forward I worried it wouldn't come. The spectators were a blur. Someone handed out orange slices and I didn't even see the hand. My stomach churned with the gel I'd taken at mile twenty-two. A runner passed me and my heart jolted, as if he'd taken the time from me. I kept doing the math out loud under my breath, muttering numbers between gasps, and they kept coming out too close to call.

Kenji had never been at the front of a marathon before, but with one mile to go he was in fourth place, and the realization made his breathing go strange. He wasn't supposed to be here. He was an amateur with a day job at a printing company. The three runners ahead of him were professionals with sponsors on their singlets. He could see the pace car's flashing lights. Television cameras on a motorbike swung round toward him, and he felt his face go hot under the sweat. What if he collapsed on camera? What if he went too fast and burned out and dropped to tenth? He kept looking over his shoulder, which wasted energy, he knew it wasted energy, but he couldn't stop checking for the runner in red he'd passed at mile twenty-three. His arms were swinging stiffly. His mouth was parched no matter how much he swallowed. Each kilometer sign seemed to take twice as long to arrive. He could hear his own heartbeat over the crowd.

The last mile wound up a long, gradual hill, and Beatriz had been dreading it since the course map came out. She'd walked it last week and her stomach had dropped just seeing it. Now she was at the bottom, and her hip had been aching since mile eighteen, a dull insistent throb that sharpened each time her right foot landed. She'd promised her daughter she'd finish. Her daughter was at the top of the hill with a handmade sign. Beatriz kept rolling her shoulders to loosen them. She glanced at the runners around her, all of them seeming steadier, stronger. What if her hip gave out? What if she had to walk, or limp, in front of her girl? The thought made her eyes sting. She sucked on her water bottle though it was empty, just to have something to do with her mouth. Her fingers kept clenching and unclenching at her sides. Halfway up, she heard someone shout her name and she lifted her head, her chest fluttering.

This is my first marathon, and I didn't think I'd make it this far, and now that I have, I'm somehow more wound up than at the start. One more mile. My body feels wrong in a hundred small ways: a hot spot on my left heel that's surely a blister, a stitch flickering under my ribs, a dizziness every time I turn my head. I'm Priyanka, I started running two years ago after my divorce, and finishing this has become tangled up with everything else in a way I can't untangle right now. What if I fall? People fall in the last mile. I've seen the videos. I keep scanning the road ahead for potholes, cones, anything that might trip me. My hands have gone tingly. I tell myself to breathe deep and it comes out as a hiccupy gasp instead. The crowd is cheering, "You've got this!" and I want to believe them, but my legs are trembling, and I keep checking my watch, not for the time but for my heart rate, which is climbing.

Declan had passed the twenty-five-mile marker four minutes ago and there was still no sign of his wife in the crowd. She'd said she'd be at the last mile. She'd promised. He scanned the faces on both sides of the road, swiveling his head left, right, left, his pace stuttering every time he turned. Had something happened? Had she gotten lost on the subway? She'd been feeling sick that morning, pale, waving it off. His throat tightened. He told himself she was fine, she was just further up, and kept moving, but his legs felt clumsy now, as if his mind had stopped steering them. A volunteer held out a cup of water and he took it and spilled most of it down his shirt. He kept squinting at every flash of a blue jacket. His breathing had gone ragged and uneven, and it had nothing to do with the miles. When he spotted the finish arch ahead and still hadn't seen her, his stomach dropped, and he lengthened his stride without meaning to.

"Biscuit! Biscuit, come!" Nora's voice cracked on the second shout, and she cleared her throat and tried again, louder. Nothing. The backyard was dark beyond the reach of the porch light, and the gate, she now saw, was open a few inches, swaying in the wind. She hadn't left it open. Had she? She shoved her feet into her husband's boots, three sizes too big, and clomped out across the wet grass with her phone flashlight bobbing. Her heart was pounding. She shone the light under the deck, behind the shed, into the gap by the compost bins. Each empty space made her stomach twist tighter. Biscuit was old and half deaf and terrified of cars. The road was only a block away. She went to the gate and stood in it, calling, her voice thin in the cold air. A car passed on the main road, its engine rising and falling, and she held her breath until the sound faded. Then she called again, shaking the treat bag hard, its rattle sounding pitiful in the dark.

I let Rufus out at nine, like always. Ten minutes, max, and he scratches at the door. It's been twenty-five. I've been standing at the kitchen window with the dish towel twisted in my hands, staring at the yard. The fence is six feet. He can't jump it. He can't. I keep telling myself that. My name is Ezra, I live alone, and Rufus is the only thing in this house that's glad to see me when I get home. I open the back door and whistle. My whistle comes out weak. I whistle again and the neighbor's dog barks back, which isn't what I want. I step onto the patio in my socks, which immediately soak through, and I don't care. I check behind the grill, the little hollow under the hydrangeas where he likes to lie. Nothing. My breath is coming quick and shallow and fogging in front of my face. I go back inside for a flashlight and can't remember which drawer it's in, opening one after another, rattling utensils, my hands clumsy.

The twins were already in their pajamas when their father realized Pepper hadn't come back in. Oluwaseun stepped out on the back step and called, keeping his voice casual for the kids' sake, but his eyes were moving fast over the yard, the flower beds, the dark corner by the rain barrel. No small white shape. No jingling tags. Behind him, one of the twins asked, "Where's Pepper?" and he said, "She's just sniffing around, go brush your teeth," and heard the slight wobble in his own voice. He walked the fence line, running his hand along the boards, feeling for a loose one. His pulse was quick and high in his chest. There, near the back corner, a dug-out patch of earth, fresh, just large enough for a small terrier. His stomach dropped. He crouched and stared at it. Beyond the fence lay the wooded ravine, black and enormous at night. He thought of the coyotes the neighbors had mentioned. He stood up too fast, nearly slipping on the wet grass, and fumbled for his phone.

Mrs. Albescu had let Bruno into the yard while she watched her program, and when the program ended and she went to let him in, the yard was empty. She stood at the door with her hand on the frame for a long moment, not understanding. Then she called his name. Her voice, at eighty-one, did not carry the way it once had. She called again. The garden was small, enclosed on three sides by the walls of neighboring buildings, and there was nowhere for a dog to hide, and yet he wasn't there. Her heart began to flutter, an irregular little trembling she felt in her neck. She went out in her slippers, leaning on her cane, peering behind the potted lemon tree, the bench, the stack of old flowerpots. Nothing. She noticed then that the narrow side door to the alley stood ajar. Who had opened it? The delivery boy? Her hand tightened on the cane until her knuckles ached. She stood at the alley door, peering into the dimness, calling his name again and again, softer each time.

It started raining around eight, and I figured Maxi would come scratching at the door any second, because she hates getting wet. She didn't. I opened the door and called. The rain was hammering the patio so hard I could barely hear myself. I grabbed an umbrella and went out, and it was useless against the wind, flipping inside out within seconds, so I dropped it on the steps and walked out bare-headed. My name is Siobhan, I'm twenty, and Maxi was my childhood dog who came with me to my first apartment, and she's thirteen now, and she's slower than she used to be. I kept picturing her lying somewhere, hurt, unable to get up. I checked under the porch on my hands and knees, mud soaking my jeans. Nothing. My heart was racing and my hands kept shaking as I swept the phone light over the bushes. Every gust rustling the hedge made me spin toward it, hoping. I kept calling her name until my voice went hoarse and scratchy.

Zhang Wei had stepped inside for a single phone call. Five minutes, maybe seven. When he came back out onto the deck, the yard was quiet and Lucky's water bowl sat untouched beside the steps. He scanned the lawn. Lucky was a big dog, a shaggy shepherd mix, impossible to miss. Unless he wasn't there. "Lucky?" No answer. Zhang Wei went down the steps two at a time. He walked the perimeter quickly, then more slowly, studying every inch of fence. All intact. The gate was latched. So where?
