His mind kept supplying answers he didn't want: someone had taken him, he'd been poisoned, he'd crawled away somewhere. Zhang Wei's mouth was dry. He rubbed his palms against his trousers again and again. He checked the shed and found it locked, of course, and then unlocked it anyway with fumbling fingers, just in case. Empty. He stood in the middle of the lawn, turning slowly, his breath loud in his ears, then went back to the gate and checked the latch once more.

Backstage, Olivia couldn't stop flexing her fingers. Open, close, open, close. The cellist beside her was calmly reading a novel, and Olivia envied her so much it was almost a physical ache. Through the curtain she could hear the hall filling up, the dense murmur of four hundred people finding their seats, the occasional cough echoing off the high ceiling. Her bow was resting on her knee and she checked the rosin on it for the fifth time. Her violin was perfectly tuned; she'd tuned it ten minutes ago and then again five minutes ago. She plucked the A string softly, just to be sure. It was fine. Of course it was fine. Her stomach was doing slow, queasy flips, and she wished she hadn't eaten anything at all. The stage manager poked her head in and said, "Two minutes," and Olivia's heart lurched so hard she had to press her hand against her chest. She stood, smoothed her black dress, and found her knees weren't quite reliable beneath her.

My hands are cold. That's the thing nobody tells you about stage fright, that your hands go cold as ice right when you need them most, and I'm a pianist. I'm sitting on a folding chair in the wings, holding my fingers under my armpits to warm them, while the act before me finishes. I'm Samuel. I'm seventeen. This is the regional competition, and the judges' table is a long white rectangle just visible from where I'm sitting, three people with pens. One of them yawned during the last performer's piece, and I keep wondering if he'll yawn during mine. I run the opening of my Chopin in my head and get to the tricky passage in bar twelve and my mind goes blank. Blank. I can't remember the next note. My stomach drops through the floor. I go back to the beginning and play it again in my head, fingers twitching in my lap, and this time it comes, but now I don't trust it. I hear applause and someone touches my shoulder. My turn.

The bar was smaller than Abdul had imagined, which somehow made it worse. A big hall, you could disappear into. Here the audience sat close enough to touch, maybe thirty people at little round tables, nursing drinks, half of them looking at their phones. His first open mic. He tuned his guitar against the back wall and the strings felt too slippery under his fingertips. He'd written the song himself, about his grandfather, and suddenly it felt far too personal to sing to strangers. What if they talked through it? What if they laughed? He kept clearing his throat, testing his voice, and each time it came out a little scratchy. He took a sip of water, then another. The host was introducing him. He walked to the stool and sat down, and the microphone was set too high, and he fumbled with the stand, adjusting it with a loud metallic screech that made everyone wince. His ears were burning. He stared at the fretboard, his throat tight, counting himself in under his breath.

Miriam had played the oboe in the same community orchestra for twenty years, and she'd never once had a solo. Tonight she did, sixteen bars in the second movement, exposed and alone. All through the first movement she sat with her reed in her mouth, keeping it moist, and every time she swallowed she worried she was drying it out. Her left foot was tapping the floor, not to the beat. She made it stop. It started again. She could feel her pulse in the tips of her fingers where they rested on the keys. The conductor turned the page and Miriam felt the second movement approaching like a train in a tunnel, the rumble growing. She checked her music. Her solo was circled in pencil, and the pencil marks seemed to throb on the page. Her mouth was dry as paper. She glanced into the dark audience and caught a glint of her husband's glasses in the third row, and her stomach clenched tighter still. The strings began their soft introduction. She raised the oboe.

I play drums in a wedding band, have for years, so I didn't expect this. But tonight's wedding is my ex-girlfriend's, of all the cruel coincidences, and the bandleader didn't know until we'd signed the contract, and I couldn't afford to pull out. So here I am behind my kit in the corner of a ballroom, waiting for the first dance. I keep adjusting my throne, up a notch, down a notch. I've tightened the snare twice. My sticks are slick in my hands; I wipe them on my trousers, and they're slick again in seconds. I'm Rhys, I'm usually the one cracking jokes between sets, and tonight I haven't said a word. The bride's family keeps looking over. Or I think they do. My foot is twitching on the bass pedal and I have to lift it off so it doesn't accidentally thump. When the bandleader counts us in, my first stroke lands a hair too early, and the sound of it rings in my ears, and I feel my face go hot.

Ten minutes before she was due on stage at the folk festival, Aiyana went looking for a quiet spot and found none. Every corner backstage had someone in it: a fiddler warming up, a sound tech swearing at a cable, a kid with a juice box. She ended up behind a stack of amplifier cases, crouching with her back against the canvas tent wall. She could hear the crowd outside, thousands of them, a sea of sound rising and falling. Her stomach was churning so badly she thought she might actually be sick, and she breathed in through her nose, out through her mouth, the way her vocal coach had taught her. It didn't work. Her hands were trembling, and she clasped them together so tightly her rings dug into her fingers. She hummed the first line of her opening song and her voice shook. She hummed it again. Still shaking. Somebody called her name from across the tent. She stood up too fast, and the world swam for a moment, and she grabbed the top amp to steady herself.

The box on Rebecca's doormat had no return address. Just her name and apartment number in block capitals, written with a thick black marker, and a postmark from a town she'd never heard of. She stood in the hallway looking down at it for a long time before she picked it up. It was lighter than she expected. Something shifted inside with a soft thump, and she nearly dropped it. She carried it into the kitchen held out in front of her, at arm's length, and set it on the counter, then took a step back. Who knew her address? She'd moved here eight months ago specifically so certain people wouldn't. Her mind flicked through possibilities and every one of them made her chest tighten further. She checked the deadbolt behind her. She picked up her phone, thought about calling someone, and couldn't decide who. Her pulse was thudding in her ears. She found the kitchen scissors and held them over the tape, the blades hovering, her hand not quite still.

I don't order things online. Ever. So when the courier knocked and handed me a heavy package addressed to me, I signed for it with a scrawl and then stood in the doorway long after he'd gone, holding it against my stomach. My name is Ignatius, I'm sixty-eight, and I'm a creature of routine. Unexplained things unsettle me deeply. I set it on the dining table and circled it. It had a label from some company I didn't recognize, a string of letters that meant nothing. I put on my reading glasses and studied the label again. Still nothing. Was it a scam? I'd read about those, people sending things and then demanding payment. My heart was beating faster than it had in months. I phoned my daughter and got her voicemail, and my message stumbled over itself, ending with "call me back, it's probably nothing." Then I sat across from the box, my hands folded tight on the tablecloth, and waited for the phone to ring, glancing from the box to the phone and back.

Jamal's roommate was out, and the package had his name on it, and it was ticking. Very faintly, but ticking. He held his ear close to the cardboard and listened, holding his breath. Tick. Tick. Tick. He straightened up so fast he banged his head on the cabinet above the counter. He rubbed the spot, eyes fixed on the box. It was just a clock, surely. Someone had sent him a clock. Who sends a clock without a note? His thoughts went immediately to every movie he'd ever seen, and his stomach clenched. He backed away to the other side of the room and stood by the window, arms crossed, then uncrossed, then crossed again. He pulled out his phone and typed "ticking package what to do" into a search bar and then felt so foolish he deleted it. But he didn't go near the box either. He texted his roommate: "did u order anything?" and stared at the screen, his thumb tapping its edge, while the faint ticking went on and on.

The package was from her father. Klara knew the handwriting instantly, the cramped left-leaning letters he'd always written with, and her knees went loose under her. They hadn't spoken in six years. Not a word. She'd changed her phone number. She'd moved twice. And somehow, here was his handwriting on her doorstep. She sat down on the front step right there, the box on her lap, and couldn't make herself go inside. Her breath was coming fast and shallow. The cardboard was soft at the corners, worn, as if it had been sitting somewhere for a long time before being mailed. What was in it? An apology? An accusation? Something of her mother's? Each possibility pulled at a different place in her chest. She ran her thumbnail along the edge of the tape, not cutting it, just tracing it, back and forth. A neighbor walking a dog said hello and Klara looked up, startled, and said hello back in a voice that didn't sound like hers. Her fingers were trembling against the box.

It was a small padded envelope, no bigger than my palm, with a customs sticker from Brazil. I don't know anyone in Brazil. I'm Henrik, I work in IT security, and I spend my days warning people about exactly this kind of thing. So I didn't open it. I put it on the shelf by the door and went to make dinner, and then found myself walking back to look at it three times before the pasta was done. I photographed the label and zoomed in on every character. I searched the sender's name. Nothing. My palms were sweaty and I kept wiping them on my jeans. I ate standing up in the hallway, plate in hand, eyes on the envelope. It felt lumpy, something hard and small inside. A USB drive? My mind went immediately to the worst possible version. My shoulders were rigid. I slept badly, and twice in the night I got up and checked that the envelope was still on the shelf, as if it might have moved on its own.

Imani's mother called the package "a mystery gift" and was delighted, but Imani, nineteen and newly home from her first semester, felt something cold settle in her stomach when she saw the return label. It was from the university. The registrar's office. Why would the registrar send a box? A box, not a letter. Letters were for grades. Boxes were for, what, returning your things? Expelling you? She'd failed a midterm in October and never told anyone. Her mother was beaming, offering her the scissors. "Go on, open it!" Imani laughed, a short brittle sound, and took the scissors, and set them down again on the table. "In a minute. I want to put my bag away first." She carried the box to her room and shut the door and sat on the bed with it between her knees. Her heart was going so fast it felt like a hummingbird's. She stared at the shipping label, reading her own name over and over, swallowing hard against the lump climbing her throat.

Nobody wanted to be the first to open the cedar chest. It sat at the foot of Grandma Concetta's bed where it had always been, and the three siblings stood around it in a loose, awkward triangle. Antonio kept clearing his throat. Giulia had her arms folded tight across her chest, fingers drumming on her elbow. And Matteo, the youngest, hovered near the door as though he might bolt. They all knew what was in there, or thought they did: the jewelry, the will, the deed to the house in Calabria that nobody could agree about. They'd argued over the phone for a month. Now, standing in their grandmother's room with her perfume still faintly in the air, Antonio felt his heart thudding. One wrong word and the whole family could split like an old board. He reached for the latch, and his hand hovered. Giulia's breath caught audibly. He glanced at her, then at Matteo, and swallowed. "Okay," he said, and his voice came out cracked, and he tried again.

My sister and I hadn't been alone in a room together for three years, and now we were alone in Nana's attic, sorting her things into boxes labeled KEEP, DONATE and ASK. I was hyperaware of everything Hazel did, every sigh, every pause. When she picked up Nana's sewing basket, I tensed. I'd wanted that basket. Would she take it? Would I say something? I'm Gwen, I'm the older one, and I'm supposed to be the one who keeps the peace. My stomach was in a knot. I kept my eyes on the shoebox of photos in front of me and sorted them without really seeing them. My hands were busy but clumsy; I dropped a stack of old postcards and they fanned across the floorboards. Hazel bent to help me pick them up. Our fingers nearly touched over a picture of the two of us as kids in matching swimsuits. We both froze. I could hear my own breathing. I didn't know if she was going to laugh or cry or leave, and I couldn't find a single word.

Ji-ho found the envelope tucked inside a hymnal while his brothers were packing up their grandmother's bookshelf. On the front, in her shaky hand: For Ji-ho only. He felt the blood drain out of his face. He glanced at Min-jun and Dae-sung, who were bickering over a lamp, and quickly slid the envelope into his jacket pocket. Why only him? What would his brothers think? There'd been talk in the family about money, about who had visited her the most, about who had borrowed what. His palm stayed pressed flat against his pocket as though the envelope might jump out. His heart was racing. He tried to keep packing but kept putting books in the wrong box. Dae-sung said, "You okay? You look pale," and Ji-ho said he was fine, just dusty in here, and coughed unconvincingly. He felt like a thief. He kept glancing at the door. When Min-jun turned toward him, his hand jerked away from his jacket so fast he knocked a stack of books off the shelf, and they crashed to the floor.

Maribel had been dreading the jewelry box for days. It was the last thing left, and it was the one thing Abuela had never clearly divided. The four cousins gathered at the kitchen table where they'd eaten a thousand Sunday dinners, and Maribel set the box in the middle, and nobody touched it. Her cousin Esperanza was twisting a paper napkin into a tight rope. Her brother Rafael kept clicking a ballpoint pen. Maribel's own knee was bouncing so hard the table trembled slightly, and she pressed both hands on her thigh to still it. She knew Esperanza wanted the gold crucifix. She knew Rafael's wife had her eye on the pearl earrings. And she, Maribel, wanted the little silver ring Abuela had worn every day, worthless to anyone else, but she wasn't sure she could say so out loud. The silence stretched. Someone's stomach growled and nobody laughed. Maribel opened her mouth, closed it. She reached for the lid, and three pairs of eyes snapped to her hand.

Oskar and his two half-sisters had met exactly twice before the funeral. Now they were sharing their grandmother's tiny flat for a week, sorting through a life that had overlapped with each of theirs in different, unequal ways. He was acutely aware that she had raised them and only visited him at Christmas. Every item he picked up, he glanced at Freya or Astrid before deciding where to put it. Was he allowed an opinion on the clock? On the photographs? He kept his voice low and his sentences short. When Freya asked if he wanted anything in particular, he said, "Oh, no, whatever you think," too quickly, and then hated himself for it, because there was something: a small painted bird their grandmother had once sent him, its twin standing right here on the windowsill. He kept glancing at it. His face felt hot. He folded a cardigan very carefully, then refolded it, putting off the moment when he'd have to ask. His heart was beating far too hard for a question about a wooden bird.

I found the will at the back of Granny's bureau, in a manila envelope marked IMPORTANT, and the moment I read it I knew it was going to wreck us. It left the cottage to me. Only me. Not to my brother, who'd done the hospital runs, not to my sister, who'd paid for the care home. Me. The youngest, the one who lived abroad and visited twice a year. My name is Niamh, and I stood there in the bedroom with the paper rustling in my shaking hands, listening to Ciaran and Orla laughing about something downstairs. They had no idea. My mouth was dry and I couldn't swallow. I read it again, as if the words would rearrange themselves. They didn't. I thought about shoving it back in the drawer. I thought about tearing it up. My pulse was hammering in my temples. Orla called up the stairs, "Niamh, tea's ready!" and I nearly dropped the envelope, and my answer came out so high and strange that there was a pause downstairs before she called again.

Raymond turned the key in the lock at 8:52 and his hand was already damp. This was the first Monday since the new superstore had opened two blocks down, and he'd spent the whole weekend imagining his customers drifting toward its bright glass doors and their cheap parking. He flipped on the lights. The hardware shop looked the same as always: bins of nails, the paint counter, the smell of sawdust and oil. It felt smaller somehow. He set out the sandwich board on the sidewalk and straightened it, then straightened it again. Across the street, a woman walked by with a shopping bag from the superstore, and Raymond's stomach dropped. He went inside, booted up the register, and counted the float twice, losing his place both times. He kept glancing at the door. At nine, no one. At 9:05, no one. He wiped down a counter that was already clean. Every car that slowed outside made him look up, his breath catching, and every car that drove on made his shoulders sink a little further.

I opened the bakery late this morning because my head baker quit on Friday, by text, and I've spent the whole weekend learning his sourdough from scribbled notes. I'm Nkechi, I own the place, and I'm a pastry person, not a bread person. The loaves came out of the oven at seven, and they look okay, I think. Maybe a little flat. Maybe a lot flat. I kept pressing the crusts and listening for the hollow sound, and I couldn't tell if what I heard was right. Now it's 7:30 and the doors open at eight, and the Monday regulars come for that sourdough specifically. Mr. Patterson has bought the same loaf every Monday for six years. I could feel my heart picking up every time I thought about his face. I arranged the loaves in the basket, flattest at the back. I rearranged them. I cut one open to check the crumb and my knife hand wasn't steady. When I saw the first shape at the door, peering in, I froze behind the counter, flour on my apron.

Ahmed found the shop's front window cracked when he arrived Monday morning, a long jagged line running corner to corner like a frozen bolt of lightning. Nothing seemed missing. The phones were in their cases, the tablets on their stands. But the crack meant someone had tried, and the thought sent a cold wave through his chest. He stood on the sidewalk with his keys in hand, unable to unlock the door. What if someone was still inside? He peered through the glass, cupping his hands against it, scanning the shadows behind the counter. His breathing had gone shallow. He called the police non-emergency line and was put on hold, and stood there listening to tinny music, shifting from foot to foot, glancing up and down the empty street. When he finally went in, he flipped on every light at once and walked through the stockroom with a broom gripped in both hands, feeling ridiculous and unable to put it down. Every creak of the old building made him freeze. He checked the back door three times.

Chloe had inherited the flower shop from her aunt three weeks ago, and this was her first Monday opening it alone. Her aunt had left a binder of instructions, and Chloe had read it twice over the weekend and still had a dozen questions, none of which she could ask. She unlocked the door and the bell above it jingled, a sound that used to mean visiting her aunt and now meant she was in charge. The cooler hummed. She checked the temperature: right? She thought it was right. She looked it up in the binder anyway. The Monday order sheet said a delivery of lilies was due at nine, and she'd never received a delivery, never signed for anything, didn't know where they went. She swept the floor while she waited, then swept it again. Her stomach was too tight for breakfast. When the delivery van pulled up and the driver hopped out with a clipboard, she wiped her hands on her apron and went to meet him, already apologizing before he'd said a word.

The inspector was coming on Monday. Somewhere between nine and noon, the letter said, which meant three hours of not knowing. I'm Gustavo. I've run this little restaurant for eleven years, and we've passed every inspection, but last month the walk-in fridge broke down for half a day and I'm still not sure I threw out everything I should have. I came in at six, two hours earlier than usual. I scrubbed the grill until my arms ached. I checked the date labels on every container in the walk-in, and then checked them again, lifting each lid, smelling, putting it back. My stomach was churning so badly I couldn't drink my coffee. Every time a car pulled into the lot, I went to the front window and peered through the blinds like a man in a spy film. My line cook came in at eight and asked if I was okay, and I snapped at him, which I never do. Then I apologized. Then I went back into the walk-in and checked the labels again.

Ewa's bookshop had a single unpaid invoice from her largest supplier, sixty days overdue, and on Monday morning there was an email waiting with the subject line FINAL NOTICE in capital letters. She read it standing in the doorway with her coat still on, the keys still dangling from the lock. Her coffee sat untouched on the counter, steam curling up and fading. She'd meant to pay it. Things had just been so slow since summer. She checked her business account on her phone and the balance made her throat tighten. She unlocked the till and counted the cash inside even though she knew exactly how much was there. She opened the shutters and the morning light fell across the shelves, across all the books she'd ordered with such hope, and now they looked like debts with spines. A customer came in, an older man, and she said good morning with a smile that felt stretched and wrong, and when he asked for a title she couldn't remember which shelf it was on.

It was Tariq's first shift at the food bank, and within ten minutes he'd already dropped a crate of canned beans. They rolled everywhere, under tables, between people's feet, and he scrambled after them, muttering apologies, his face blazing. The coordinator, a brisk woman named Pauline, told him not to worry, but she said it while already walking away, and he couldn't tell if she meant it. He was stationed at the distribution table now, handing out bags, and the line stretched out the door into the cold. Every person who stepped up, he wanted to say the right thing and wasn't sure what that was. Should he smile? Would smiling seem condescending? Should he make eye contact? He kept fiddling with the edge of his volunteer badge. When an elderly man asked whether there was any rice, Tariq didn't know, and he turned around to look and then turned back, and the man was waiting, patient, and Tariq felt his throat close up. "Let me, um, let me find out," he managed.

I'd volunteered at food banks before, but never at the one in my own neighborhood. I hadn't thought about what that meant until the third person in line was my son's piano teacher. She saw me and her face did something, a flicker, and then she looked down at the floor. My stomach dropped. I'm Wendell, a retired accountant, and I'd never had to think about what it felt like to be on the other side of this table. Suddenly I was aware of everything: my clean jacket, my watch, the way I was standing behind the table like a shopkeeper. I wanted to make it okay for her and I had no idea how. I fumbled the bag as I handed it over and a carton of eggs nearly slid out. We both grabbed for it. "Thank you," she said quietly, not looking up. I said, "Of course," and my voice came out too loud, too hearty, and she flinched, and I wanted to sink straight through the floor. My hands didn't stop trembling for an hour.

The food bank had run out of baby formula by eleven, and there were still forty people in line, and Jacinta was the one assigned to tell them. She was seventeen and here for her school service hours. She hadn't signed up for this. The coordinator had handed her a stack of printed sheets listing other places to try, and squeezed her shoulder, and left. Jacinta stood at the front of the line holding the sheets against her chest like a shield. Her heart was pounding so hard she could see her shirt move. The first woman with a baby on her hip stepped forward, and Jacinta opened her mouth and nothing came out. She swallowed and tried again. "We, um. I'm really sorry. We're out of formula today." The woman's face fell, and Jacinta felt it like a blow. Her eyes started to sting. She held out one of the sheets with a shaking hand, and the paper rattled faintly in the air between them as the woman stared at it.

Big Lou ran the loading dock at the food bank like a drill sergeant, and on his first Saturday, Pavel was assigned to work under him. Lou barked instructions faster than Pavel could follow, half of them in slang Pavel didn't know; his English was good, but not that good. Pallet jack, shrink wrap, the back-of-house cage. Pavel nodded at everything, terrified of asking, and then stood there not knowing which pallet to move. His shirt was soaked through despite the cold air blowing in from the open bay doors. He kept watching Lou out of the corner of his eye, trying to anticipate what he wanted. When Lou yelled, "Hey, new guy!" Pavel's whole body jolted, and he nearly backed the pallet jack into a stack of crates. Lou stared at him. Pavel's stomach sank into his shoes. He opened his mouth to apologize, and Lou just pointed at a different pallet and said, "That one, buddy," and Pavel moved toward it with his legs stiff and his heart still hammering.

We'd organized the Thanksgiving drive for months, and on the morning of distribution, the delivery truck carrying three hundred turkeys was two hours late. I'm Hye-jin. I'm the volunteer coordinator, so everyone kept looking at me. Volunteers were asking what to do. The line outside was already around the block, and I could see people stamping their feet in the cold. I kept calling the dispatcher, and every time it went to a recorded message I felt my chest squeeze a little tighter. I paced between the front door and the loading dock, back and forth, until one of the older volunteers gently put a hand on my arm and said, "Sit for a second." I couldn't sit. I set up extra tables we didn't need. I counted the boxes of stuffing mix. I counted them again because I'd lost track halfway. I kept chewing my bottom lip until it was raw. When I finally heard a big diesel engine rumbling outside, I ran to the window, my whole body leaning toward the glass, praying.

Corinne had been a social worker for thirty years and retired in June, and she'd thought volunteering would be easy. She was used to need. But at the food bank intake desk, she had to ask people for their address and household size, and something about sitting behind the clipboard made her chest tight in a way she hadn't anticipated. A young father stood before her with a sleeping toddler on his shoulder, and when she asked his income, his jaw tightened. She hadn't meant to embarrass him. Had she? She stumbled over her next question. Her pen skipped. She wrote the wrong number in the wrong box and had to cross it out, and the crossing-out looked so harsh on the page that she felt her cheeks go warm. She kept clicking the pen, a small rapid tick, until she realized she was doing it and put it down. Behind him, the line was growing longer. She could feel every pair of eyes. She smiled at the toddler, then worried that seemed patronizing, and stopped.

The waiting room clock was ten minutes fast, or maybe it was slow, and Graham had decided he couldn't trust it, so he kept checking it against his phone. Four hours since they'd wheeled his wife into surgery. The doctor had said three, maybe three and a half. He sat on the hard plastic chair, then stood, then sat again in a different chair, as if a new angle might bring news faster. A vending machine hummed in the corner. He'd bought a packet of crackers an hour ago and it sat unopened on the seat beside him. Every time the double doors swung open, his head snapped up, and every time it was someone else's nurse calling someone else's name. His leg jiggled. He pressed his hand on it. It jiggled harder. A family across the room was laughing quietly about something, and he wanted to ask how they could, and also envied them. He pulled out his phone, read the same text from his daughter three times without taking it in, and put it away.

I've been in this chair for so long that the vinyl has stuck to the backs of my legs. My brother was in a motorcycle accident this afternoon. That's all they've told me: accident, surgery, someone will update you. I'm Farah. I came straight from work and I'm still wearing my lanyard and I keep fiddling with it, twisting the strap around my finger until it pinches, letting it go, twisting it again. The fluorescent lights hum. There's a television on the wall playing a game show, and the laugh track makes my skin crawl. I can't stop looking at the door. Every time someone in scrubs walks through it, my heart seizes and I half rise out of my seat before I see they're heading to someone else. My mother is on a plane from Karachi and I'm the only one here, and I have to be the one to hear whatever they say. My mouth tastes sour. I keep drinking from a paper cup of water that I've crushed half flat in my fist.

Sven sat in the children's hospital waiting room surrounded by brightly painted animals on the walls, a cheerful giraffe grinning down at him, and he had never felt so far from cheerful in his life. His four-year-old had swallowed something, a battery, they thought, and now she was in with the specialists, and he was out here. He was holding her stuffed rabbit, which she'd dropped when they took her through. He kept smoothing its ears flat, over and over, until the fur was matted. His chest felt tight and fluttery at the same time, like a bird was trapped in there. He couldn't sit still. He walked to the window and looked out at the parking lot and walked back and sat down. A nurse passed, and he half stood, opening his mouth to ask, and she gave him a small apologetic shake of the head without stopping. He sat again. His wife was on her way from the airport; he'd called her, and his voice had broken on the phone, and he couldn't stop hearing that.

Mrs. Nakamura had brought her knitting, as she always did, but her needles had been still for twenty minutes. Her husband had gone in for what the cardiologist called a routine procedure, and routine procedures, in her experience, did not take this long. She looked down at the half-finished scarf in her lap. She'd dropped a stitch somewhere and hadn't noticed. She tried to find it and couldn't focus. Her eyes kept sliding to the reception desk, where a young man in scrubs was typing and occasionally answering the phone. Each time the phone rang she straightened in her chair, sure it was about Kazuo. It never was. She smoothed the yarn, wound it around her finger, unwound it. Her chest felt tight and her breathing was quick and shallow, and she made herself take a long slow breath, the way her yoga teacher said, and it shuddered on the way out. She glanced at her watch. Then at the clock. They didn't agree, and that small discrepancy bothered her far more than it should have.

The ER waiting room at two in the morning was full of coughing and crying children and a man holding a towel to his bleeding hand, and somewhere behind those swinging doors was my best friend, Destiny, who'd collapsed at the party and hadn't woken up when we shook her. I came in the ambulance. They didn't let me go back. I'm Keisha, I'm nineteen, and I'm not family, so nobody will tell me anything. I keep going up to the desk and asking anyway. The woman there is tired and not unkind, but she just says "I'm sorry, honey," and I go back and sit down. I'm still wearing my party dress and I'm freezing, my arms covered in goosebumps, my teeth almost chattering. I can't stop replaying it. Had she taken something? Had I missed something? I've texted her mom five times. My leg won't stop bouncing. Every time the doors open I'm on my feet before I know I've stood up, scanning faces in scrubs for any sign at all.

Father Augustine had sat in hospital waiting rooms with a hundred families over his years as a priest, offering steady words and folded hands. Tonight it was his own sister in the operating room, and he found that none of his steadiness had come with him. He kept taking his rosary out of his pocket and putting it back without praying. His collar felt tight; he ran a finger around the inside of it. The coffee from the machine was bitter and too hot and he drank it anyway, burning his tongue, barely noticing. A young couple sat across from him, and the woman glanced at his collar with a kind of hope, and he felt a hot rush of shame that he had nothing to give her right now. He looked away. He stood and went to the window. The parking lot lights glowed orange through a light drizzle. He watched the raindrops slide down the glass, counting them, losing count, starting over, his breath fogging the pane, his hands clasped too tightly behind his back.
